title: We adapt
hook: we get used to good and bad fortune; a famous lottery study was small but influential

segments.voice: Yesterday: the science of savoring, staying with a good moment forward, now and looking back. Your line was savor. Did you take one mental photograph? Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

The new phone is a marvel. The screen is so bright, the camera so sharp. For a while. Then one ordinary morning it's just the phone, and there's a crack in the corner, and a newer one is on a billboard. The same thing happens with a raise, a bigger apartment, a new town. And, more surprisingly, it can happen with losses too. People get used to things. Researchers have a name for it, and one old, small study that made it famous. Today: we adapt.
screen: `THE NEW PHONE IS A MARVEL.` → `THEN IT'S JUST THE PHONE.` → `GAINS, AND LOSSES TOO.`

segments.voice: First, the study. Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman interviewed lottery winners, people who had been seriously injured in accidents, and a comparison group of neighbors, and published it in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. The winners were no happier than the comparison group. And they took a little less pleasure in ordinary things: chatting with a friend, hearing a joke, a compliment. Second, the other half. The people who'd been injured rated their present happiness lower than the comparison group, but not as low as one might guess. Researchers call this pull back toward where we started hedonic adaptation, sometimes the hedonic treadmill. Third, the correction. The study was small, and it's been retold so often that it's grown in the telling. Researchers have kept testing the idea, and some argue that people don't always adapt all the way back; some losses can leave a lasting mark. So the careful version is: we adapt, often more than we expect, but not always completely. Fourth, an old practice built on this. The Stoic teacher Epictetus told his students to remember what a thing really is, so it can't ambush them. Even when you kiss your child, he said, remember that you love a mortal being. It sounds bleak. It's meant to do the opposite: to keep familiar things from going invisible. Adaptation dulls the good. Noticing can wake it back up. We adapt.
screen: `WINNERS NO HAPPIER, A STUDY FOUND.` · `THE INJURED, NOT AS LOW AS GUESSED.` · `SMALL STUDY; NOT ALWAYS ALL THE WAY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WHAT A THING REALLY IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing you've got used to. Sit comfortably and breathe. Look around the room, or around your life, for something good that has gone quiet from being familiar. Running water. A friend who always answers. Your own two hands. Your morning light. Pick one, and look at it as if it had arrived today. Stay with it for the whole sit. The bell holds the time.
We adapt. Good fortune and bad both pull us back toward where we started, often more than we expect, though not always completely. Today's word.
Your line: we adapt. Today, pick one ordinary thing you've stopped seeing, and give it a second look at least once. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some contemplative traditions use deliberate noticing, such as giving thanks for ordinary things or the Stoic habit of remembering that what we love is passing, to keep familiar goods from going unseen.

fork.reveal: the winners were no happier than the comparison group, and ordinary pleasures landed a little lighter. a small study, but the pattern of adapting has held up in part.

trapdoor: what you thought: winning the lottery would change everything.
what it means: people tend to adapt to good and bad fortune, drifting back toward where they started.
what a scholar hears: hedonic adaptation. the classic lottery study was small; later work finds adaptation is real but sometimes incomplete, especially after some losses.

sources.ref: Brickman, P., Coates, D., and Janoff-Bulman, R., "Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative?" Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1978)

notes: Check the summary of Brickman et al. (1978): lottery winners, accident victims and a control group; winners not significantly happier than controls and reporting less pleasure from mundane events (talking with a friend, hearing a joke, receiving a compliment); accident victims lower than controls but less low than might be expected.

'Later research suggests people don't always adapt all the way back', with illness and long unemployment as examples, follows later longitudinal work (e.g. Lucas); a reviewer may want a specific citation added.
Epictetus, Enchiridion 3 (the earthen pot and kissing one's child) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the paraphrase is fair.
The term 'hedonic treadmill' is attributed to researchers generally, without a date.
